reason: The sources reliably support a surprising space myth-busted story with over ten verified claims and corresponding Wikimedia visuals.
story: For centuries, a persistent myth has claimed that the changing phases of the Moon are caused by Earth's shadow blocking the Sun. But this is completely false! The true cause has nothing to do with our planet casting a shadow. Instead, the Sun constantly illuminates half of the Moon, while the other half stays in darkness. As the Moon travels along its orbital path around Earth, our perspective shifts. From our viewpoint, we see varying portions of that sunlit side, creating everything from a delicate crescent to a brilliant full moon. Earth's shadow only touches the Moon during a rare lunar eclipse, which happens about twice a year. The next time you gaze up at a glowing crescent, remember you are watching a cosmic game of shifting angles, not Earth getting in the way.
angle: The changing phases of the Moon are not caused by Earth's shadow, but by our shifting perspective of its sunlit side.

claims.claim: The Moon's phases are not caused by Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.
The Sun continuously illuminates half of the Moon while the other half remains in darkness.
The synodic period or cycle of lunar phases takes approximately 29.5 days.
The Moon's orbital sidereal period around Earth is about 27.3 days.
Earth's shadow only affects the Moon during specific events called lunar eclipses.
Lunar eclipses happen roughly twice per year.
The Moon is tidally locked to Earth and always shows the same face toward us.
There is no permanently dark side of the Moon; both sides experience day and night.
Lunar libration allows terrestrial observers to see about 59 percent of the Moon's surface over time.
The Warren Field calendar in Scotland is nearly 10,000 years old and tracks lunar phases.
The four major phases are the new moon, first quarter, full moon, and last quarter.

disputed: Whether the Warren Field site represents the absolute oldest known formal calendar in human history (attribute to researchers like Professor Vincent Gaffney).
